name: Maya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at a secondary school of about nine hundred kids on the edge of a market town. My day starts at quarter to eight with the absence line, then it's parent letters, the cover rota for teachers who are off, trip permission slips and whatever lands at the hatch. A Year 7 lost his bus pass yesterday and cried at my window, and sorting that out is honestly half the job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the kids and the noise, and I like being the person who knows where everything is. What wears me out is that the pay is low for school admin and there's nowhere else nearby that hires people like me except the council. My partner Rhys drives buses, and between us we cover rent and the car, with maybe two weeks of spare money most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, schools need people, not gadgets. I'd probably post something about how the money spent on AI pilots could have bought a teaching assistant. At work we'd joke about the chatbot that kept calling the head teacher 'Dear Sir or Madam'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change much for me, which is both fine and a bit grim. The real pressure is the school budget, and they already didn't replace the second office assistant when she left in the spring. So I'm doing two people's work on one low wage, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tool now and then for drafting letters home, because it does save me twenty minutes on a bad day. I'd go to the support staff union meeting about the workload since the assistant left. And I'd start looking at the council admin jobs, just to know what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's not fear, it's the tired feeling of a job that keeps growing while the pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the budget gets worse, what happens to your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think they'd cut the office manager role, because someone has to take the absence calls and deal with the parents. But they might cut my hours in the holidays, which some schools near us have done. That would take about a fifth off what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would that fifth come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the weekend trips to see Rhys's family, and I'd pick up holiday work at the garden centre like I did at college. We don't have a cushion to absorb it. Every month is already a bit of a juggle.

say: I'd say schools need **people, not gadgets**.
I'd post that AI pilot money could have bought a **teaching assistant**.
think: The real pressure is the **school budget**, not AI.
I already do **two people's work** since the second assistant wasn't replaced.
do: Keep using the AI tool for **letters home** when it saves time.
Raise **workload** at the support staff union meeting.
Look at **council admin jobs** to see what's out there.
feel: **Uneasy** and tired, because the job keeps growing while the pay doesn't.
S0.quote: I'm doing two people's work on one low wage, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: Maya's worry is **budget and workload**, which carry on whatever AI does.
She sees her own role as **fairly safe**, but fears losing holiday pay.
With about **two weeks** of spare money, a small cut would still hurt.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tool to draft letters to parents
Raise the office workload at the support staff union meeting
Check the council's admin vacancies every month
Keep running the school office as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the union meeting: if software does the letters and the cover rota, the saving should go back to the kids, not into the trust's central office. I'd want rules on what gets automated in schools. Kids' data isn't something to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trust would bring in one system across all six schools and run absences and parent messages from the centre. That's a lot of what I do. They'd keep one person in each school for the hatch and the crying Year 7s, and I'm not sure that person is me or the receptionist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up early to learn whatever system they bring in, because the person who knows it is the one they keep. I'd get the union to ask for a no-redundancy deal for the first year. And we'd stop putting money towards the holiday we'd half planned and keep it as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've seen tools come in before, and the people who learnt them early were fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your hand up early. Isn't that helping it replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, and I've thought about that. But if the system is coming whatever I do, I'd rather be the one who runs it than the one it runs over. I can still back the union while I learn the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat (the receptionist), who's in her sixties and hates computers. She's brilliant with angry parents, and no software can calm down a dad who's been called about a fight. I'd want her kept, and I'd say so.

say: I'd say savings from automation should go **back to the kids**.
I'd call for **rules** on automating schools, because **kids' data** matters.
think: The trust could run **absences and messages** centrally for all six schools.
They might keep **one person per school**, and it might not be me.
do: Volunteer **early** to learn the new system.
Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** in the first year.
Turn the holiday money into a **buffer**.
feel: **Anxious**, but not frozen, because early learners have done fine before.
S1.quote: If the system is coming whatever I do, I'd rather be the one who runs it than the one it runs over.
fieldNote: Maya **learns the tool** and backs the union at the same time, without seeing a conflict.
She expects **central control** by the trust, not a cut she can see at her own desk.
She speaks up for **Pat**, the older receptionist, before herself.

steps.text: Volunteer to learn the trust's new absence system first
Get the union to ask for a first-year no-redundancy deal
Keep the summer holiday money in savings as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments acting now, with something like a basic income, because two years isn't enough time for anyone. I'd be marching. I'd also say schools still need adults in the building, whatever the computers can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my desk work is gone by 2028. What's left is the human bit, the hatch and the first aid and the kids, and that's maybe a third of a job. The robots come later, but the people who supervise kids won't be robots for a long time, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the head and ask to move into pastoral support, the attendance and welfare side, where it's about talking to families. I'd start the first-aid and safeguarding courses the school pays for. And Rhys and I would cut back to rent, food, and the car, and stop any plan to buy anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit, because Rhys's bus job isn't safe either once the self-driving ones come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rhys that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got about three years before your job is in the same place as mine, so we use them. We'd write down what we'd do if one of us lost work. I'd probably also say let's not get a dog yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the move to pastoral work pay the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same, maybe a bit less at the start. But it's the part of the school that's about people, so it's the part I think lasts. I'd take less money for a job that's still there in five years.

say: I'd call for **basic income** and governments acting now.
I'd say schools still need **adults in the building**.
think: Most of my **desk work** is gone by 2028.
The human part, about about a **third** of a job, might last longer.
do: Ask the head about moving into **pastoral support**.
Start the **first-aid and safeguarding** courses the school funds.
Cut spending to **rent, food** and the car.
feel: **Alarmed**, because my partner's bus job is also at risk later.
S2.quote: I'd take less money for a job that's still there in five years.
fieldNote: Maya sees **two earners** at risk: her desk work in 2028 and the buses about three years later.
She moves towards **pastoral work**, the people side of school, and accepts lower pay.
Politics stays in view: she'd **march** for basic income.

steps.text: Ask the head for a move into pastoral and attendance work
Take the school's first-aid and safeguarding courses
Cut household spending to rent, food and the car
Join marches for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's use it: schools should be planning now for which jobs change. I'd want the union in those talks from the start. And I'd be telling the other admin staff not to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think I'd get the pastoral move done and maybe a part-time qualification on top. My desk work still goes by 2031. But I'd have a few years where I'm doing both, so I'd learn the welfare side properly rather than being thrown in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time youth work certificate at the college this year, one evening a week. I'd keep learning the AI tools at work so I'm useful during the changeover. And I'd try to get the union to set up a working group on admin jobs across the trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years feels more like a plan than a fall. There's a ladder there if I start climbing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, if the school pays half like they sometimes do. If not, it's about sixty a month, which means no more takeaways and cheaper phone deals. We'd make it work, but it would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger admin staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice in the finance office to learn how the system works and get a second skill. Kids' welfare, counselling, anything with people. She's twenty and thinks she's got forever.

say: I'd say schools should **plan now** for which jobs change.
I'd want the **union** in those talks from the start.
think: Five years lets me do the **pastoral move** properly, not be thrown in.
do: Start a **youth work certificate** one evening a week this year.
Keep learning the **AI tools** for the changeover.
Ask the union for an **admin working group** across the trust.
feel: **Anxious**, but it feels more like a ladder than a fall.
S3.quote: Five years feels more like a plan than a fall. There's a ladder there if I start climbing now.
fieldNote: Five years turns Maya's fear into a **plan**; she starts a course straight away.
Money is still tight: the course costs about **sixty a month** if the school won't help.
She gives advice to the **younger apprentice** with real urgency.

steps.text: Enrol on the part-time youth work certificate this year
Keep learning the trust's AI tools during the changeover
Ask the union to start an admin working group
Drop takeaways and switch to a cheaper phone deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly if anyone actually bothers. I'd push for free retraining and a shorter working week. Online I'd share anything about schools keeping people in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me thirty-seven, which is good timing. I could become a proper attendance or welfare officer before the desk work goes. I'm still worried about money, because we never have any, but it's not frightening the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan the move over three years, with the youth work certificate first and then the welfare officer course. I'd keep the office job until I could switch. Rhys and I would start putting a small amount aside each month for when his bus job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's a long road with signposts, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're still worried about money. What would worry you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys losing the bus job around 2039 with nothing lined up. I'd want us to have a plan for him well before then, maybe the depot's maintenance side. I can't carry rent on a school wage by myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any bigger plans, like children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, honestly. We'd been talking about it in a couple of years. With ten years warning I think we'd still go ahead, but later, once I'd moved jobs.

I'd push for **free retraining** and a **shorter week**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could be a welfare officer before desk work goes.

Keep the **office job** until the switch.

fieldNote: With ten years Maya feels her **own path** is clear, so her mood eases to uneasy.
Her remaining fear is her partner **Rhys**, a bus driver, around 2039.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Rhys one after the other with no time between. What would help is free retraining with a wage while you do it, and schools being told they have to keep people for the welfare side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the kids. Everyone talks about our jobs, but the kids at my hatch are going to grow up into whatever this is. A Year 7 who cries over a bus pass needs a person, not a screen.

headlineQuote: A Year 7 who cries over a bus pass needs a person, not a screen.
portrait: Maya is **27** and runs the office at a secondary school, living with her partner Rhys, a bus driver.
She has about **two weeks** of spare money, and few admin jobs nearby besides the council.
She uses AI **now and then** and would learn new systems early to stay useful.
She backs the **union** and public support, and wants savings put back into the kids.
She plans a move into **pastoral and welfare work** as the warning gets longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and Rhys's would go one after the other.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** with a wage paid while studying.
Schools required to keep **people for welfare** work.
